prompt.context: Regional Jet Corporation is a U.S. manufacturer of regional airplanes — aircraft with 100 seats or less. Its business consists of two types of aircraft: (1) jet engine, 80- to 100-seat aircraft and (2) propeller, 20- to 30-seat aircraft. In fiscal year 1999, Regional Jet delivered 100 jet engine aircraft and 150 propeller aircraft. This represented a unit volume increase year-over-year of 10% and 5%, respectively, and revenues of $730 million and $225 million, respectively. Although overall profitability for Regional Jet in 1999 was a competitive 5% economic profit margin, profitability varied significantly by business. The prop business generated a stellar 30% profit margin, while the jet engine business was unprofitable with a margin of -3%. Over the past several years, Regional Jet has experienced eroding profitability in its jet engine aircraft business. Its prop business, despite being profitable, has been flat in most recent years. At a January 5th analyst conference, Regional Jet's senior management team announced that the company was committed to managing for value. To this end, Regional Jet has hired you and a team of consultants to help the company develop and implement value-maximizing strategies for its businesses.
prompt.question: For our case discussion today, please focus on the jet engine aircraft business: (1) How would you go about further analyzing this business? (2) What recommendations would you like to make to senior management?

clarifying_info.q: What is the size of the U.S. jet engine regional aircraft market?
clarifying_info.a: In 1999, the U.S. jet engine, 100-seat-or-less aircraft market was approximately $5 billion.

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors and what are their market shares?
clarifying_info.a: There is no dominant competitor. The market leader has 20% share. There are 4 other competitors with 12%-18% share each. Regional Jet has approximately 16% share.

clarifying_info.q: How fast is the market growing?
clarifying_info.a: The market has been growing approximately 5% (in units delivered) per year for the past 5 years and is expected to continue at 5% for the next decade. In 1999, a total of 625 jet engine regional aircraft were delivered.

clarifying_info.q: How would you describe the supplier power in this market?
clarifying_info.a: The supplier base for regional aircraft parts is highly fragmented and Regional Jet uses approximately 50% proprietary parts in its jet engine aircraft. Hence, supplier power is low.

clarifying_info.q: How concentrated is the competitive landscape among manufacturers?
clarifying_info.a: The market is fairly concentrated with only 6 jet engine regional aircraft manufacturers, so intensity of direct competition is low-to-moderate.

clarifying_info.q: Who are Regional Jet's customers and how much buying power do they have?
clarifying_info.a: In 1999, there were 225 customers, including airlines, aircraft lessors, local and national governments, businesses, and private individuals. Customer power varies by segment. Aircraft lessors make large purchases (often 20 or more aircraft per buying cycle) and exploit significant negotiating leverage over manufacturers. All other customers have low-to-moderate buying power depending on creditworthiness.

clarifying_info.q: Is there indirect competition from larger jets?
clarifying_info.a: Larger commercial jets (100 seats or greater) with longer range can be used on regional routes, but they are expensive for customers to operate solely on a regional basis. Intensity of indirect competition is low.

clarifying_info.q: What are the barriers to entry?
clarifying_info.a: Jet engine regional aircraft manufacturing requires significant capital investment in production facilities and equipment, as well as strong relationships with various labor unions. Barriers to entry are high.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average market profitability?
clarifying_info.a: The market is profitable; the average competitor has generated 4% economic profit margins over the past 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: What is Regional Jet's offering position versus competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The company's offering position is at parity. Its cockpit design is similar to the industry standard (low pilot retraining switching costs), its range of 500 miles is in line with the market average, and maintenance costs over the 20-year asset life are in line with competitors.

clarifying_info.q: What is Regional Jet's operating cost position?
clarifying_info.a: Regional Jet's operating cost per aircraft is at parity with the industry. Every jet engine aircraft delivered in 1999 cost approximately the same to produce.

clarifying_info.q: Can I see profitability broken down by customer segment?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — see the Additional Handout: Jet Engine Regional Aircraft Business Per Aircraft Economics and Profitability by Customer Segment (1999).

Note: Assumes debt-to-total capital of 70%.

(2) Profitability by Customer Segment ($mm) across three customer groups — customers who buy 1 aircraft, customers who buy 3 aircraft, and customers who buy 20 aircraft — showing number of customers, revenues, COGS, SG&A, Delivery & Other, Taxes, Net Income, Capital Charge, Economic Profit, number of aircraft delivered, and segment share.

framework: Market Economics: Assess market size, growth, and profitability; evaluate structural forces (supplier power, customer power, competitive intensity, indirect competition, barriers to entry)
Competitive Position: Evaluate Regional Jet's offering position, pricing position, and operating cost position relative to competitors
Customer Segmentation: Identify customer segments and analyze profitability by segment to pinpoint the driver of the overall business loss
Alternative Generation: Develop strategic options to restore profitability in the jet engine business
Recommendation: Select the value-maximizing strategy with supporting rationale, risks, and next steps

questions.prompt: Assess the structural attractiveness of the U.S. jet engine regional aircraft market using the five forces framework.
questions.guidance: Supplier power is low (fragmented supplier base; 50% proprietary parts). Intensity of direct competition is low-to-moderate (only 6 manufacturers, no dominant player). Customer power is mixed — aircraft lessors have high buying power due to large-volume purchases (20+ aircraft per cycle); all other customers have low-to-moderate power. Indirect competition from larger commercial jets is low (expensive to operate on regional routes). Barriers to entry are high (capital-intensive, requires union relationships). Overall the market is structurally attractive and the average competitor earns 4% economic profit margins.

questions.prompt: What does Regional Jet's market share growth of 10% (vs. market growth of 5%) in a parity-offering, parity-cost business tell you about its pricing position?
questions.guidance: Because Regional Jet has a parity offering and parity operating costs yet is growing share faster than the market, it must be pricing below the market average. It is pricing for share, i.e., it has a disadvantaged pricing position. This explains the negative economic profit despite a profitable market.

questions.prompt: Calculate the average revenue per aircraft for each customer segment and identify the key driver of unprofitability.
questions.guidance: Operating cost per aircraft is identical across all segments (parity operating position), so the only variable driving segment profitability is price. Compute revenue per aircraft for each segment to confirm the lessor segment is priced significantly lower.

math.setup: Revenue per aircraft = Segment Revenue / Aircraft Delivered for each segment
steps: Lessors pay ~$1.2-1.6mm less per aircraft than other segments
Total economic cost per aircraft = $7.858mm (from Per Aircraft Economics table)
Lessor revenue per aircraft ($6.8mm) < total economic cost per aircraft ($7.858mm) => each lessor aircraft destroys value
Non-lessor segments are above economic cost per aircraft and generate positive economic profit
math.answer: Aircraft lessors receive an average price of $6.8mm per aircraft vs. $8.4mm (buy-1) and $8.0mm (buy-3). The lessor segment generates -$33mm economic profit, fully explaining the jet engine business's -$20mm total economic profit (the other two segments together earn +$14mm, netting to -$19mm, approximately consistent with the -$20mm total).

questions.prompt: If Regional Jet pursues new small and medium non-lessor customers at the market growth rate of 5%, how long would it take to double the economic profit of the jet engine aircraft business?
questions.guidance: The candidate must recognize the current jet engine economic profit is -$20mm (not yet positive), so 'doubling' requires first achieving positive profit, then doubling it. This alternative faces a slow road to profitability. The candidate should flag that 5% unit growth per year from non-lessor customers is modest relative to the 60 lessor units (60% of volume) that would need to be replaced, and the timeline is likely a decade or more — making this an unlikely path to rapidly doubling business value.

math.setup: Current economic profit = -$20mm. Positive economic profit per non-lessor aircraft can be computed from segment data: Buy-3 segment earns $11mm EP on 35 aircraft = ~$0.31mm EP per aircraft. Current non-lessor aircraft = 40 (5 + 35). At 5% growth per year on ~40 non-lessor aircraft = 2 additional aircraft per year. At ~$0.31mm EP per aircraft, incremental EP per year ≈ $0.6mm. Starting from -$20mm, it would take approximately 33 years just to reach breakeven — far too long to be viable.
steps: 5% growth per year: 40 x 5% = 2 additional aircraft/year
EP per non-lessor aircraft (blended): ($3mm + $11mm) / (5 + 35) = $14mm / 40 = $0.35mm per aircraft
Incremental EP per year from 2 new aircraft: 2 x $0.35mm = $0.70mm
Years to close -$20mm gap at $0.70mm/year: 20 / 0.70 ≈ 29 years to reach breakeven
math.answer: Approximately 29-33 years to reach breakeven — this alternative provides a very slow path to value creation and is unlikely to double business value in any reasonable timeframe.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the strategic option of exiting the aircraft lessor customer segment entirely and serving only small and medium customers.
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify the risk of losing scale. Lessors currently account for 60 of 100 aircraft (60% of volume). Exiting the lessor segment would drop volume from 100 to 40 aircraft. At parity operating costs, fixed cost absorption across a smaller base could raise per-unit cost above the current economic cost, eliminating profitability even in the remaining non-lessor segments. The candidate should ask: What share of costs are fixed? Can the company maintain competitive unit economics at 40 units? This option eliminates the loss-making segment but may destroy the profitable segments through diseconomies of scale.

questions.prompt: Evaluate the strategic option of Regional Jet entering the aircraft leasing market to improve its negotiating leverage with lessor customers.
questions.guidance: Facts: The leasing market is large and growing (nearly 50% of new aircraft delivered in 1999; expected to grow 5%/year). The market is profitable (average ROE ~15% vs. cost of equity ~10%). Three lessors dominate with 65% combined share. Key profitability driver is cost of funds — and Regional Jet would be at parity on cost of funds. Regional Jet already has marketing relationships with aircraft end-users (lessors' own customers) from the sales configuration process. Entering leasing would allow Regional Jet to (1) earn the lessor margin itself rather than ceding it via price concessions, and (2) improve negotiating leverage with the three dominant lessor customers by becoming a competitor to them. Risks include capital requirements to fund a leasing portfolio and management complexity of a new business model.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the strategic alternatives Regional Jet could pursue to improve profitability in its jet engine aircraft business?

categories.name: Pricing / Revenue Improvement
ideas: Raise prices to lessor customers to at least recover total economic cost per aircraft
Implement volume-tiered pricing that limits the depth of discount for very large orders
Develop a minimum price floor policy by customer segment

categories.name: Customer Segment Strategy
ideas: Aggressively pursue new small and medium non-lessor customers to shift segment mix
Gradually reduce lessor customer concentration by capping lessor volume
Exit the lessor segment entirely if scale can be maintained with non-lessor volume

categories.name: Vertical Integration / New Business Entry
ideas: Enter the aircraft leasing market to capture lessor economics and improve negotiating leverage
Provide manufacturer financing (vendor financing / operating leases) more broadly to end-users, bypassing lessor intermediaries
Acquire an existing aircraft lessor to rapidly gain leasing capabilities and market relationships

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Increase scale by growing total unit volume to spread fixed costs further
Outsource non-proprietary components to reduce COGS
Streamline delivery and logistics to reduce Delivery & Other costs

categories.name: Partnership / Alliance
ideas: Form joint ventures with lessors to share economics rather than cede price
Explore co-marketing agreements with airlines to generate pull demand and reduce lessor dependence

recommendation: Regional Jet should pursue a dual strategy: (1) enter the aircraft leasing market to capture lessor margin and improve negotiating leverage with the three dominant lessor customers, and (2) simultaneously grow its small and medium non-lessor customer base to reduce dependence on the lessor channel over time

Entering the leasing market is the highest-priority action because it addresses the root cause — the pricing disadvantage to lessors — and is supported by an attractive, profitable leasing market (ROE ~15% vs. 10% cost of equity), parity cost of funds, and existing end-user relationships
Growing the non-lessor customer base diversifies revenue and reduces the structural leverage lessors hold, but should be viewed as a medium-term complement rather than a near-term substitute
risks: Capital requirements to fund a leasing portfolio may strain Regional Jet's balance sheet
Management focus and capability risk of operating a leasing business alongside manufacturing
The three dominant lessors may retaliate by reducing or eliminating purchase orders if Regional Jet becomes a direct competitor in leasing
Scale risk: if lessor volume declines before non-lessor volume scales, per-unit costs could rise above economic cost thresholds
next_steps: Conduct a detailed feasibility and capital requirements analysis for entering the aircraft leasing market
Identify acquisition targets or partnership structures in the leasing market that would accelerate entry
Develop a customer acquisition plan and timeline for growing the small and medium non-lessor segments
Model the P&L impact of a range of lessor-to-non-lessor volume mix scenarios to identify the minimum lessor volume compatible with profitable operations
